ob_replication_selfdescription.text: Discrimination performance increased substantially when the right hand was distant from, but moving toward the visual probe location (replicating the far-hand effect, Festman et al., 2013 ). However, this effect disappeared when the probe appeared close to the static left hand, supporting the view that static and dynamic features of both hands combine in modulating pragmatic maps of attention.

ob_participants.text: A convenience sample of five participants (age: 20–27, 2 male, all right handed) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in the experiment.

ob_configuration.text: Their left hand was placed near the lower right side of a keyboard placed left of display.

ob_interaction.text: We found a significant interaction of hand proximity and movement direction when the probe was presented to the right of fixation; mean performance was significantly higher when the participants' hand was under the left side of the display (far proximity) moving toward it (rightwards), compared to when moving away from it (leftwards) [82.6 vs. 72.3%, F (2, 8) = 4.494, p < 0.05, see Figure 3D ].

ob_left_null.text: No significant effect of movement direction was found in trials with left probe [ F (1, 4) = 0.348, see Figure 3C ].

ob_independent_contribution.text: The present study, by simply placing observers' other hand near the turning point of the hand movement, reduced the resulting far-hand effect again, therefore suggesting that attentional pragmatic maps are dynamically delimited by the current positioning of both hands, as was proposed by Rizzolatti et al. ( 1994 ).

h_originals_distinguished.text: The interplay of near-hand and direction effects was examined in a subsequent study by Festman et al. (2013b) , in which the right hand moved below the display, while the left hand remained stationary on the side. A direction effect was only present for letter probes on the right side.

h_joint_prediction.text: Furthermore, on the basis of the direction effect of Festman et al. (2013a , b ), we predicted better discrimination when moving toward the probe in both tasks.

h_left_configuration.text: Average viewing distance was 52 cm and they were instructed to rest their left hand in their lap.

h_experiment2_same_apparatus.text: The apparatus and software were identical to Experiment 1.

h_temporal_direction.text: Specifically, it revealed a hand proximity effect in (partial) accordance with MVP but no further modulation of hand proximity by movement direction.

h_spatial_direction.text: The effect of Direction was significant for small gap trials, t (24) = 1.89, p < 0.05, d = 0.38 (one-tailed), and medium gap trials, t (24) = 1.79, p < 0.05, d = 0.36 (one-tailed), but not for large gap trials, t (24) < 1, ( Figure 2B ).

h_right_handed_subset.text: The repeated-measures ANOVA with the within-subjects factors Direction (toward and away), Proximity (near, intermediate, and far), and Gap Size (brief, medium, and long) on accuracy in right-handed participants did not replicate the interaction between Direction and Gap Size, F (2,44) = 1.90, p = 0.16, η p 2 = 0.08.

h_current_overlap_explanation.text: Festman et al. (2013b) have previously shown that stationary and dynamically moving hands combine in their effect on visual selection. Since participants in the present study were instructed to rest their left hand in their lap, the two hands of a participant were closest together whenever the right hand reached the central position under the display, which reflects our intermediate hand proximity condition.

h_joint_replication_statement.text: We observed evidence for a directionality effect in the spatial gap discrimination task, as reflected in enhanced performance when moving toward as compared to moving away from the probe, which provides a replication of the previously established directionality effects in spatial tasks ( Festman et al., 2013a , b ).

h_separate_gozli_target.text: Since this hypothesis has, so far, only been tested with static hand postures, we provide a conceptual replication of Gozli et al.’s (2012) result with moving hands, thus also probing the generality of the direction effect.

h_overlap_inference.text: As a consequence, there was a partial overlap of pragmatic maps from the left and the right hands, which might explain enhanced performance at intermediate proximity.

original_identity.title: Synergistic effects of temperature, salinity and light on the hermatypic coral Montipora verrucosa

subject_data_finding_chains.subjects_data: Publisher abstract describes Montipora verrucosa, short-term thermal tolerance affected by salinity/light, and long-term growth experiments. Exact sample sizes, treatment levels and original curves cannot be verified without full original.
subject_data_finding_chains.published_finding: Publisher abstract supports light aggravating high-temperature injury; it also describes worse pigment, mortality, carbon fixation and growth under strong light near both thermal extremes. This is not solely a salinity claim.
subject_data_finding_chains.current_test: Current 2017 experiment crosses ambient versus heated water with full sunlight versus 50% shading, including M. capitata (historical M. verrucosa), and measures growth/bleaching/mortality. It expressly groups 1978 among experiments being replicated and cites it in the irradiance discussion. No separate 1978-specific directional hypothesis is stated in the inspected current text.
subject_data_finding_chains.finding_link: There is an explicit cited conceptual connection and an empirical temperature-by-irradiance manipulation. Absence of salinity manipulation or old recovery measurements cannot alone establish absence of conceptual retesting. Full original is needed to align the particular original light/temperature contrasts and data with the current contrasts.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence: Current calcification does not vary with irradiance; reported light mortality effect is during recovery.
No 1970 recovery measurements reported; historical comparisons use full-sun conditions.
1978 is also cited for historic tank temperature variability.
Publisher abstract establishes a light/temperature finding, but not its exact experimental provenance or independence from other original reports.
subject_data_finding_chains.unresolved: 1978 full methods/results and cross-report data overlap are unavailable; no report-count or replication classification made.

original_identity.title: Thermal Tolerance in Tropical versus Subtropical Pacific Reef Corals

subject_data_finding_chains.subjects_data: Original field observations date to 29 August–3 September 1974 at Enewetak, plus controlled 16-liter flow-through aquarium experiments at Enewetak and Hawaii within weeks of one another. Sustained heating and repeated 34°C shocks were tested. Table 1 separately gives Enewetak versus Hawaii conditions; Hawaiian temperature groups are 27.1°C/96h, 31.3°C/95h, 32.4°C/50h, with three colonies per each of five species per group. Figure 2 also combines earlier studies, including Jokiel et al. in press, with present data.
subject_data_finding_chains.published_finding: Enewetak corals tolerate about 2°C higher absolute temperature than Hawaiian congeners; field and lab evidence connects tolerance to regional thermal history. The report contains new 1974 data AND a multi-source survival synthesis.
subject_data_finding_chains.current_test: Current study tests Hawaii in 2017 against historical Hawaii results; it does not sample Enewetak. Its discussion expressly uses the 1976 regional difference as an analogy to the observed historical shift. Its methods nevertheless groups 1976 with the replicated early series.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence: Original is not merely a bibliographic duplicate of a 1970 Hawaiian experiment: it includes new regional comparative experiments in 1974.
Shared series citation does not by itself establish retesting of the geographic comparison.
Current historical threshold inquiry and original geographic thermal-history inference are conceptually related.
subject_data_finding_chains.unresolved: No coding decision. The regional comparison and Hawaii-only temporal comparison must not be conflated.

original_identities.title: Continuous hand movement induces a far-hand bias in attentional priority
Both hand position and movement direction modulate visual attention

subjects_data.2013a: 11 participants; concealed right-hand leftward-and-return movements; contingent masked T/L probes; response with same mouse. Near/intermediate/far proximity crossed with toward/away direction. Original reports no proximity main effect, a direction effect (78.4% toward versus 76.8% away), and proximity-by-direction interaction. Source is publisher PDF web extraction, not locally saved PDF bytes. Left-hand location is not specified in the inspected original method; do not invent lap placement.
subjects_data.2013b: New convenience sample of five; concealed moving right hand plus stationary visible left hand beside keyboard to display left; T/L discrimination answered with left hand. Direction/proximity interaction for right-side probes (far toward 82.6% vs away 72.3%); no direction effect for left-side probes. It explicitly identifies the far-hand component as replicating 2013a, while interpreting suppression near the static left hand as its added finding.
subjects_data.current: Experiment 1 temporal gaps, Experiment 2 spatial gaps; concealed moving right hand, left hand in lap, responses with right-hand mouse. Same apparatus in both experiments. Current hand motion starts from either side on separate trials rather than a compulsory right-left-return sequence. Current text nominally reports samples 25 and 23 but several statistical degrees of freedom imply other counts; retain source as supplied, no repair.

finding_links.link_type: Explicit replication claim in full original 2013b; independent participant sample, shared published direction finding.
Jointly cited prospective prediction and jointly cited replication statement. Current spatial task tests toward-versus-away benefit; temporal task lacks direction modulation.

Current discussion explicitly invokes 2013b and proposes overlap of left-lap and moving-right-hand maps as an explanation. This contrary evidence is preserved: 2013b is not cited only for direction. Current design does not manipulate left hand beside display versus absent/lap; it does not reproduce 2013b left-side suppression configuration.

shipped_identity.title: Hand position alters vision by biasing processing through different visual pathways
shipped_identity.scope: Supplied row identifies separate static-hand temporal/spatial proximity hypothesis. Current calls its moving-hand tests a conceptual replication of this finding. Gozli original full text was not separately acquired in this focused task.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence: Distinct DOI and new sample establish distinct reports/experiments, not necessarily distinct retested findings.
2013b explicitly replicates 2013a direction finding; current cites both for a single direction prediction.
Current also invokes 2013b static/dynamic integration for the temporal intermediate-proximity pattern.
Current reports weak/marginal direction evidence and a right-handed-only accuracy subset that does not retain the Direction-by-Gap interaction. Statistical source inconsistencies left untouched.
subject_data_finding_chains.unresolved: Closest-chain choice and whether current exploratory overlap account constitutes a separately retested 2013b finding are reserved for parent; no classification or report-count decision.
